# A note on jacobians during integral transformations 
Jacobians arise wherever there are multidimensional integral transformations. In the current case, transformations are done for depth averaging, i.e. the following splitting of integrals 

$$
\int_V = \int_S \int_0^{h} \lvert J \rvert 
$$ 

Notice the requirement to compute the Jacobians $J$. However, for surfaces with mild curvatures, the discrete elements are planar. The planar geometry of such meshes have an added advantage. Both the global and local coordinate systems are Cartesian. This means that the Jacobian used for coordinate systems, expressed as, 
$$ 
J = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_1} & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_2} & \frac{\partial f_1}{\partial x_3} \\ \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x_1} & \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x_2} & \frac{\partial f_2}{\partial x_3} \\ \frac{\partial f_3}{\partial x_1} & \frac{\partial f_3}{\partial x_2} & \frac{\partial f_3}{\partial x_3} \end{bmatrix}
$$ 

can be solved analytically. Here $\mathbf{f}$ and $\mathbf{x}$ represent local and global coordinate systems. Since both the global and local coordinate systems are of the same type, they can be expressed as, 
$$ 
f_1 = J_{11} x_1 + J_{12} x_2 + J_{13} x_3 
$$
$$
f_2 = J_{21} x_1 + J_{22} x_2 + J_{23} x_3 \\
$$
$$
f_3 = J_{31} x_1 + J_{32} x_2 + J_{33} x_3 
$$

or more conviniently, 
$$
    \begin{bmatrix} f_1 \\ f_2 \\ f_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} J_{11} & J_{12} & J_{13} \\ J_{21} & J_{22} & J_{23} \\ J_{31} & J_{32} & J_{33} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}$ is the jacobian. But how we calculate the jacobian? We only have the numerical values of the coordinate vectors and not their variable representations. Here's where the Cartesian nature of both coordinate systems comes handy. Because both the local and global coordinate systems are Cartesian, the local coordinate system can be represented as a 3D rotation of the global system and can be expressed simply as
$$ 
f = R x 
$$ 

where $\mathbf{R}$ is expressed as, 

$$ 
\mathbf{R} = \begin{bmatrix} f_1 \cdot x_1 & f_1 \cdot x_2 & f_1 \cdot x_3 \\ f_2 \cdot x_1 & f_2 \cdot x_2 & f_2 \cdot x_3 \\ f_3 \cdot x_1 & f_3 \cdot x_2 & f_3 \cdot x_3 \end{bmatrix}
$$ 

is the direction cosine matrix (DCM). Since the DCM's are orthogonal, their determinant is $1$. This means that the Jacobian of the coordinate transformation also has the determinant $1$. This enables us to ignore the transformation determinants when transforming integrals.
